framing: Permissions have to follow every copy of the text
paragraphs: An operations analyst may read the incident checklist and the escalation FAQ. A security-only runbook answers their signing-key question more directly. Ranking it first would improve similarity and break access control. Permission has to be resolved before protected text reaches any ordinary code.

The first search is only the start. A summary can keep a restricted fact, an old group membership can outlive a revocation, and a buffered answer can depend on a source it never cites. Evaluation exports and review queues make more copies, and each one needs its own access decision.

We follow a small multi-tenant corpus through those changes. You will compare filtering in the application with filtering in trusted retrieval, apply a missed revocation to every chunk, and check a derived report against all of its sources.

Release decisions then bring security and answer quality back together. Eligible sources, factual support, output handling, and what tools may do all need their own checks. The same distinctions return when source material and reviewed corrections become data for adapting a model.
outcomes: Enforce tenant and document permissions before protected text leaves trusted retrieval.
Keep revocations, chunk copies, and derived reports in line with current source policy.
Recheck permissions on the full context, and govern outputs, tools, caches, and evaluation exports.
question: Which protected copy could survive after the original grant has been revoked?
